The Yijing, or I Ching—the Book of Changes—is an ancient Chinese divination text and philosophical classic. Compiled over centuries and reaching its canonical form around the tenth century BCE, it describes patterns of change in nature and human affairs through 64 hexagrams, serving as a guide to understanding transformation and balance.

The text is composed of the Ten Wings, a set of commentaries attributed to Confucius, and the core Yijing text itself, organized around 64 six-line symbols called hexagrams. Each hexagram consists of six broken, or yin, lines or unbroken, or yang, lines, representing complementary cosmic principles and their dynamic interplay.

The Yijing is used as a divination tool. Practitioners cast yarrow stalks or coins to generate random hexagrams, then interpret the resulting pattern and associated texts. The Yijing describes 64 possible human and cosmic situations, each with commentary on its meaning and line-specific wisdom.

The philosophical foundation rests on the idea that the cosmos is in constant flux. Change follows patterns, and harmony comes from recognizing and adapting to these patterns. The Yijing influenced all major Chinese philosophical schools—Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism—and shaped Chinese cosmology, medicine, and martial arts. Confucius is traditionally credited with writing the Ten Wings commentaries.

The Yang and Yin symbol itself derives from Yijing cosmology, representing dynamic balance and cyclical transformation. The text shares emphasis on cosmic order, or li, and the balance of complementary forces with the Tao Te Ching. It deeply influenced Taoist cosmology and the concept of wu wei, action aligned with natural change. The Yijing is still widely consulted for divination and self-reflection today, and it is studied as a philosophical text in academic and esoteric contexts worldwide.
